nodes.referent: Robert Hooke (1635-1703), English natural philosopher, architect, and polymath; Curator of Experiments for the Royal Society of London and later Gresham Professor of Geometry. In Micrographia (1665), examining a thin slice of cork under a compound microscope he built and improved himself, he observed a honeycomb-like array of tiny box-like pores and named them 'cells' after the small rooms (cellulae) of monks -- the first published use of the word in this biological sense, though what he actually saw were the empty walls of dead plant tissue, not living cells with contents. Also known for Hooke's law of elasticity, early telescopic astronomy, arguing that fossils were the organic remains of once-living creatures, horology, and architecture (as Christopher Wren's assistant rebuilding London after the Great Fire). Sole intended referent is this 17th-century Royal Society natural philosopher -- not any other person named Robert Hooke, and not to be conflated with the plant genus or any modern namesake.

nodes.referent: Marcello Malpighi (1628-1694), Italian physician and biologist, professor at Bologna, Pisa, and Messina, and later personal physician to Pope Innocent XII; one of the first scientists to make systematic, sustained use of the microscope to investigate biological fine structure. Discovered pulmonary and other capillaries, completing William Harvey's account of blood circulation by finding the missing structural link between arteries and veins, and described fine tissue structures across many organs and organisms -- the excretory tubules in insects that bear his name (Malpighian tubules), structures in the kidney and spleen also named for him (Malpighian corpuscles/bodies), and the layered structure of skin. Also conducted detailed microscopic studies of plant anatomy (Anatome Plantarum) and of the silkworm and chick embryo. Widely credited in general reference works as a founder of microscopic anatomy / histology. Not to be confused with any other bearer of the Malpighi surname, nor with the plant genus Malpighia or family Malpighiaceae named in his honor.
